title: Besides These, Is There Another?
aliases: What the Tide Brings and the Sun Takes
logline: A bare granite dome and the wide terrace under it, where a monk stopped a king with four questions about a tree before he would teach him anything, and where the spot is still marked by a slab of rock inside a railing with mango trees planted round it.
human_question: When I say the name of something, how much of what I am left holding is the thing in front of me, and how much is the word and the two halves the word has just sorted the world into?

place.what_kind_of_place: A low granite hill standing on its own at the edge of a dry-zone plain, still a working pilgrimage site and not a ruin. It is climbed by a long ceremonial stairway of broad, shallow granite steps in a series of flights, several terraces deep, under frangipani that drop flowers onto the stone. The top opens into a wide, flat, sandy terrace named after a tree: a small white dome in the middle of it, ringed by two rows of tall octagonal stone pillars left from a roof that is gone, a headless standing Buddha and a much-worn figure of a king at the edges, and a low railed enclosure around a slab of bare rock. Mango trees are planted on and around the terrace. Immediately beside it the hill finishes in an unbroken dome of grey granite with an iron handrail running up its back, and from the top of that rock the whole plain is open, with the white domes of the old capital standing out of the forest on the horizon. Shoes come off on the upper terrace and stay off.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off. The stairway: a hundred metres of flat granite at a time, so shallow and so wide that the flights read as drawn lines going up through the trees, empty and misted at first light, with flowers on the steps. The rock: a single swell of bare stone the size of a building, with nothing on it but a handrail, which takes hard low light better than anything built. And the view off the rock, which is the reason to be there — a dry-zone plain of unbroken low forest running out past the limit of the lens, with heat beginning to move over it, and four or five distant white domes on the skyline as the only things in it that are not trees. Down on the terrace the scale reverses completely: bare feet on warm sand, a double colonnade of pillars throwing long shadows across a worn slab of rock, and a mango hanging at eye level.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Light, heat and fruit, and none of it on the crew's schedule. Mist sits in the plain before sunrise and burns off within the hour. The pillar shadows walk across the sand and across the railed slab and off it again. The bare rock goes from cold grey to orange and back to grey inside forty minutes at either end of the day. Over weeks the mango trees carry flower, then hard green fruit, then ripe fruit, then nothing; the film needs fruit on the tree, which is a matter of a few weeks in the year and not a matter of a day. Pilgrims arrive all day and thin out at midday because the granite gets too hot to stand on barefoot.
place.when_it_looks_best: The fruiting weeks, roughly March to June on this side of the country, because the film has a mango on a tree in it and there is no substitute. The first and last hour of light for the stairway, the rock and the plain; the middle of the day only for the heat coming off the granite. Deliberately outside the festival month, when the hill takes tens of thousands of people in a night: that road and that crowd belong to another film in the series, and this one needs the place ordinary and mostly empty. The dry months give the haze and the hard light; the inter-monsoon rains give cloud and green, and would cost the wide shot the horizon.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A slow, hot, very beautiful hour on one hill: up an old stone stairway through frangipani at first light, out onto an open terrace among pillars, and up a bare rock to a plain that runs out of focus before it runs out of forest, with a handful of white domes on the skyline to say how far away the old capital is. It has a shape of its own — bottom to top, close to far, cool to hot and back again — and it ends on one piece of fruit on one tree. Someone who hears none of the narration gets a complete piece with a climb, an opening out, and a return.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a transcript with pictures. The voice does not interpret the place; it reads out four questions and their answers, which is all the chronicle gives, and the pictures supply what each question is pointing at. The name comes with the fruit in close-up. The class comes with the plain full of trees. The two halves come with the far horizon. And the answer that breaks the trap comes with the slab of rock inside its railing, at the one spot where the thing being argued about was standing. The viewer is not told that a name is not a thing. They watch a king be examined on it, and pass.

sequence.on_screen: Just after first light at the bottom. Ground level, dead centre, looking straight up the line of the stairway: broad shallow granite steps in long flights climbing out of the trees, frangipani trunks either side, fallen flowers and leaf litter on the stone, thin mist still in the canopy. Two or three people far up it, small enough to be scale and nothing else.
sequence.voice: The chronicle says that a little over two thousand years ago a king came up this hill after a stag, which was the mountain's own god in that form, and met a monk who had come through the air from the mainland to teach him. The monk did not teach him. Not yet. He looked round for something to point at, and asked the king the name of a tree.

sequence.on_screen: The top of the last flight. The terrace opens out: flat sand, a small white dome, two rings of tall octagonal pillars standing without a roof. The camera crosses it and settles on a mango tree at the edge, then closes until the frame holds one fruit hanging, sharp, with the pillars soft behind it.
sequence.voice: The chronicle gives the exchange almost as a transcript. What name does this tree bear, O king. This tree is called a mango. One question, one answer, and two separate things have already come into the room. There is a tree. And there is a word that makes the tree known. The old books count both of those as concept, the thing made known and the thing that does the making known, and they are careful that these are not one item. And the chronicle had already given this ground a name meaning the mango place, a chapter before anybody asked.

sequence.on_screen: From the top of the bare granite dome beside the terrace, looking out and slightly down. The plain: unbroken low dry-zone forest to the horizon, thousands of crowns in one frame, not one of them separable from the next. Heat already moving in the air over it.
sequence.voice: Is there another mango besides this one. There are many, said the king. And there they are. In the time it took him to say that, the word stopped belonging to the tree the two of them were standing under. It is out over the whole plain now, and it will collect anything that answers to it for as far as you can see.

sequence.on_screen: Same position, longer lens. Individual crowns picked out of the canopy one at a time — a tamarind, a palu, the fan of a palmyra — then a slow pan to the far skyline, and, if the haze allows it, the white domes of the old capital standing up out of the forest.
sequence.voice: And besides this mango and those other mangoes, are there other trees. There are many, sir, the king said, but those are trees that are not mangoes. Now the word has split every tree in the country in two: the ones it gathers up and the ones it turns down. Neither half is a thing you could take apart. What the books list is smaller. A tree is on their list, and so is a fruit: a height, a spread, a roundness, that the mind reads off the way the stuff of it is laid out.

sequence.on_screen: Back down on the terrace, barefoot, camera low and close: the slab of bare rock inside its railing, stone worn smooth and pale, the shadow of a pillar lying across it, a few fallen leaves on it, the trunk of a mango tree just at the edge of frame.
sequence.voice: Then the trap. And besides those mangoes, and those trees that are not mangoes, is there yet another tree. Between them the two halves have accounted for everything there is. The answer that sounds correct is no. The king said: there is this mango tree, sir. Thou hast a shrewd wit, O ruler of men. The two halves had swallowed the plain. They had not swallowed the tree he was standing under, and he would not let go of it.

sequence.on_screen: The granite dome from the terrace in late light, filmed when it is clear: one unbroken swell of grey and orange rock with an iron handrail running up its spine and nothing else on it, the terrace and the railed slab small below. Then a static wide holding the empty rock as the light comes off it.
sequence.voice: He put the same question again, and the second time it was not about trees. Have you kinsfolk. Many, sir. And are there people who are not your kin. More of those than of mine. And besides your kin and all those others, is there anybody else. There is yet myself, sir. Good, said the monk, thou hast a shrewd wit. The books keep that answer on the same list as the mango. A person is on their list too: a name laid over body and mind taken together.

sequence.on_screen: Last of the afternoon on the terrace. Pillar shadows long across the sand and bending up the base of the rock. Then the mango tree again, whole this time, ordinary, in full sun, fruit against a pale sky.
sequence.voice: Only after that did the teaching start, and the discourse he chose was one built on the footprint of an elephant. That is how the whole of it was done. One of these books says outright that the everyday words were picked on purpose — being, person, tree, mountain, river — so that the people listening could follow easily. The first lesson this chronicle gives here was given with a tree, in the plainest words anybody had.

sequence.on_screen: Last light, and the third beat run backwards as one continuous move: the whole plain, then in and down across the forest, the terrace, the pillars, the railed slab, the tree, until the frame holds a single mango in fruit and nothing else. Hold on it until the light has gone off it.
sequence.voice: Nothing in this was taken away from anybody. The tree is not less of a tree for having a name, and the books do not say that it is; they are careful to say that some things are exactly what they are all the way down. What they say is that the word was never the tree, and that the two halves the word made were never the trees either. And that the way back from a name is the way the king took it. Past the class, past everything the class leaves out, to this one.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C084 is not a theory this place resembles; it is the syllabus the king was examined on. The Pradeepika defines paññatti as both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25], which is exactly the pair the first question separates: a tree, and a word for it. It then lists the meaning-concepts — the collective whole, the shape, the being, the direction, the time, the space, the sign [C084-P:L27–L41] — and the second and third questions do something that list does not name: they turn a word into a class and then build its complement. Neither class is a collective in the sources' sense, which the Margaya reserves for substances joined and connected into one arrangement — table, chair, bed, chariot [C084-M:L15] — so the film does not call them heaps and does not run the cloth-and-thread test [C084-M:L7] on them. What the Margaya does list is the tree itself, and the fruit, among the shape-concepts the mind reads off the arrangement of the elements: breadth, height, roundness [C084-M:L13]. It also separates the spoken sound, which is ultimately real, from the name it conveys, which is not [C084-M:L21], and lists shape, collective, being, direction and time among the concepts felt on a basis rather than found [C084-M:L11]. Put the fourth question against that apparatus and the reason it is a trap becomes visible: the two classes between them exhaust every tree, so the classes appear to have used up the world, and the only thing left to point at is the particular tree that no class is. The king pointed at it. C001 then supplies the frame the film sits in rather than another mechanism. The Pradeepika separates conventional teaching from ultimate teaching and maps the first onto the discourses [C001-P:L47], saying that the everyday names — being, person, woman, man, tree, mountain, river — were used so that listeners would understand easily [C001-P:L51]. IDEA-0001 uses that same line to license four communities' names for one mountain; here it does a different job, because what followed the examination was a discourse built on an elephant's footprint. The test was about names and classes, and the teaching that passed it was a simile. Everyday speech was not the concession; it was the method.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the interesting direction is not from the particular up to the general, which is how the riddle is usually retold as a logic puzzle, but from the general back down to the particular, which is the only move the king actually makes. Three of the four questions build categories and the fourth asks whether anything survives them. C084 on its own gives a taxonomy and no drama; the chronicle supplies the drama and the stake, because a man was being measured on whether he could hold a name, a class and a thing apart before he was allowed to be taught. C001 keeps the film from turning that into a verdict on ordinary speech: the categories are not an error the king corrected, they are the instrument he used correctly, and the teaching that followed was given in the same ordinary words. The pairing also closes the exit the material keeps offering. It would be easy to end on 'so the tree is not really there'. The Pradeepika will not allow it — what truly exists does not change from its own nature into another [C001-P:L53] — and the last beat is written to say the opposite: the word was never the tree, which is a smaller and harder claim than the tree not being there.

concept_links.why: The digest's own machinery is the content of the chronicled exchange, item for item. Paññatti is both the thing made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25]: question one. The meaning-concepts include the shape and the concept of a being [C084-P:L27–L41; C084-M:L11], and the Margaya puts the tree and the fruit themselves on its list of shape-concepts, read off the arrangement of the elements [C084-M:L13]: question one's tree, and beat four's picture. The second round about kinsfolk ends on the concept of a being. The classes built by questions two and three are not collectives in the sources' sense: the Margaya reserves that for substances joined and connected into one arrangement, table, chair, bed, chariot [C084-M:L15], so the film does not call a scattered class of trees a whole made of parts and does not run the cloth-and-thread test [C084-M:L7] on it. And the separation of the spoken sound, which is ultimately real, from the name it carries, which is not [C084-M:L21], is why the film can film a word being said and not be filming the name. The digest's limits are load-bearing here and each one changes the film. Because the sources' existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories and not a scheme of true and false, the film never says the king's earlier answers were wrong; he was right four times, and the fourth answer is not a correction of the first three. Because a film must not tell a participant that the name they use is wrong, nobody on this hill is shown as making a category mistake by being there, and no observance is narrated as a misunderstanding of what a name is. Because 'language constructs reality' is an overreach the digest names, the voice keeps the tree, the rock and the fruit fully real throughout, and the eighth beat exists to say so out loud. The digest's flagged gap is also respected: the Pradeepika prints seven items under a heading of eight, and nothing is filled in, so the voice never claims a complete list.

The Pradeepika's division of the teaching into conventional and ultimate, with the conventional mapped onto the discourses [C001-P:L47] and given in everyday names so that listeners could understand easily [C001-P:L51], is the only thing that makes sense of what happened on this terrace after the examination: the discourse chosen was a simile about an elephant's footprint. A test about names and classes was followed by teaching in names and images, on purpose. The digest then blocks the three exits this material opens. It warns that the Margaya's flat wording, that tables and people do not truly exist [C001-M:L44–L48], is unusually easy to flatten into 'nothing is real', while the Pradeepika holds that what truly exists does not change from its own nature into another [C001-P:L53]; the last beat is written against that flattening. It says explicitly that mapping the analysis onto culture, society or identity changes its meaning, which rules out reading the king's 'there is yet myself' as a point about selfhood or social construction, so the sixth beat keeps it where the sources keep it, on the list of concepts. And it refuses the 'this is just atomism' move, since the Pradeepika places the final realities beyond ordinary human knowing [C001-P:L59] — so the film never offers the plain full of trees as a scientific taxonomy lesson. Also carried across: the Margaya defines paññatti as the name for what is held to exist by mere notion [C001-M:L48], but the digest records that this extract does not settle whether paññatti means the name or the thing conceived, so the film takes that distinction from C084, where it is stated, and not from here.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That naming something does two things at once and we usually only notice the first. It makes the thing known, and it silently sorts everything else into what the word takes and what it turns down. Nothing is wrong with either, and neither of them is the thing. The demonstration needs no belief and no doctrine: four questions, four answers, a plain full of trees and one piece of fruit on one tree, and a man who was examined on the difference and got it right.
what_must_be_real: The place, the tree and the text. The riddle is not staged: there is no actor, no reconstruction, no monk, no king, and no hands pointing at a tree for the camera. The story is carried entirely by the voice over the place, and the only things filmed are the terrace, the railed slab, the rock, the stairway and a mango tree with real fruit on it in the weeks it actually has fruit. No fruit is tied, propped, wetted or brought in. This is a living site of worship and the floor applies without exception: no act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repositioned or lit for filming, nobody is an exhibit, and no person on screen is presented as devout, moved, attained or as an illustration of anything. Nobody who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera appears in the film. The sixth beat's line about a person being a concept is never cut against an identifiable individual; its picture is the empty rock, and that pairing is a rule of the edit rather than a preference. Distant figures on the stairway or the rock appear only as scale, unidentifiable and not held. Footwear, dress and the custodians' instructions are followed by the crew as by anyone else, and the chronicle is quoted as a chronicle rather than reported as an eyewitness account.
position_hint: early, and it can follow the opening film directly: the opening has several names resting on one visible thing, and this one has a single name, the two classes it makes, and the particular thing that survives them both. It is also the group's only film whose argument is a recorded examination rather than a resemblance, which makes it a good second position while the series is still establishing that the voice reads rather than interprets. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Staging the riddle in any form — an actor, a robed figure, a reconstruction, a hand entering frame to point at the tree. It would turn the strongest thing here, that a real conversation was recorded at a real spot, into costume drama.

Presenting the chronicle as documented event. It is a chronicle written centuries after the meeting it reports, and the voice must carry that without constant hedging; 'the chronicle gives the exchange almost as a transcript' and 'the chronicle says' are the register, not 'this is what happened', and the chronicle's deity-as-stag and arrival through the air are kept whenever the arrival is told at all.

Flattening the ending into 'nothing is real'. The C001 digest names this as the easiest error with this material, and the sources keep some things exactly as they are; the eighth beat is written to refuse it and must not be trimmed into the shorter, worse line.
Reading 'there is yet myself, sir' as a point about identity, selfhood or social construction, which the C001 digest says explicitly changes the sources' meaning.
Turning the plain full of trees into a natural-history or taxonomy sequence. The C001 digest rules out the 'it is just atoms' move and the visual equivalent is a species-identification montage.
Treating the sources' existent and non-existent pairs as 'true' and 'false' names, or implying that the king's first three answers were the wrong ones.

Calling a class of trees a heap or a whole made of parts. The sources' collective concept is substances joined and connected into one arrangement — a table, a chair, a chariot — and a class of scattered trees is not one; the film uses the Margaya's shape-concepts, where tree and fruit are actually listed, instead.

Suggesting, by framing or by narration, that anybody worshipping on this terrace has misunderstood what a name is. The C084 digest forbids telling a participant that the name they use is wrong, and on a living site that limit governs the pictures as much as the words.

A second stepped-ascent-to-a-hill-shrine film. The slate already carries a film about carrying materials up to a hilltop dome by hand, and this one is not a climb film: the stairway is a single opening beat and the subject is a terrace, a slab and a question.
The fruit. A mango on the tree is a few weeks of the year and the whole close-up spine of the film rests on it; arriving outside those weeks means either no film or a dishonest one.
Crowding. Outside the quiet months the upper terrace can be full, and the film needs the slab, the pillars and the rock legible and mostly empty without anybody being moved along for the camera.
Losing the wide shot. If drone flight is refused the plain still has to read as a plain; the shots from the top of the rock have to be good enough to carry beats three, four and eight on their own.
drop_if: Filming the upper terrace cannot be done without interrupting worship, moving people along, or filming people who cannot refuse.
There is no mango tree in fruit anywhere on or beside the terrace in the window available, so the close-up spine of the film would have to be borrowed or faked.
Custodial permission for the railed enclosure and the terrace can only be had on terms that require the story to be acted out or an observance to be arranged.
Neither the top of the rock nor any legal aerial position gives a wide shot in which the plain reads as an uncountable number of trees, which is what beats three and four are pointing at.

connections.note: The opening film has four living names resting on one visible thing and does not rank them. This one has a single name and the two classes it makes, and ends by coming back to the particular thing the classes leave out. Same distinction, opposite direction, and no overlap of move: no community's usage is in question here.

Same district and same primary concept, and kept apart. That film walks between two monuments whose names outlived the loss of a building and of half a stupa's height; this one sets a name against the classes it makes and the one tree they leave out. No climb or riddle there, no ruin-scale argument here.

Both are dry-zone films about what a name covers, in different districts. That one is a single reservoir whose name says sea over basins counted as five and as three, filmed from the air at two water levels; this one is a chronicled examination on a hill terrace, filmed from the ground. No shared archetype and no shared footage.

That film takes the festival road below this hill, with the free-food stalls along it, and belongs to another group and another concept. This film never goes down the road, never touches the festival, the stalls or the giving, and is deliberately scheduled outside the festival month so the two never share a night, a crowd or a frame.

selection.reason: The group's strongest historical binding by a distance: a recorded examination on exactly the distinction C084 draws, at a spot whose name means the mango place — a name the chronicle already uses before the question is asked — and which is still marked. The location supplies both a cinematic frame and a story that no analogy could do.

review.note: Confirmed by Chathura on 2026-09-25; reset to pending on 2026-09-26 because a GRP-01 audit corrected voice lines, and decision 9 says a changed body needs judging again. The location and the film's shape are unchanged. What changed, and why: (1) Beat 1 told the arrival as fact and dropped the chronicle's framing; it now opens 'The chronicle says…' and keeps what the chronicle actually has, the mountain's deity in the form of a stag and the monks arriving through the air (Mahavamsa XIV, Geiger). (2) The record said the terrace is named after the tree in the riddle; the chronicle's own chapter XIII already uses the terrace's name for the landing place before the riddle is asked, so that claim is moved to what_is_disputed, the gloss in also_known_as, what_is_certain, why_here and the factual clause of selection.reason are corrected, and beat 2 now says, on-concept, that the ground had its name a chapter before anybody asked. (3) Beat 7 called the source of the everyday-words line 'one of the old commentaries'; it is Amaradasa Ratnapala's modern Sinhala Abhidhammartha Pradipika, so it now says 'one of these books'. (4) Beat 7 said 'the first lesson ever given on this island'; the chronicle's own first chapter has earlier visits and preaching, so it now says 'the first lesson this chronicle gives here', and 'a short one' is gone, since Cula means lesser and the discourse is not especially short. (5) Beat 4 treated 'all the mangoes' and 'the trees that are not mangoes' as heaps, a whole made of parts, and applied the cloth-and-thread test; the Margaya's collective concept is substances joined and connected (table, chair, bed, chariot; C084-M:L15), which a class of scattered trees is not. The beat is rewritten on the Margaya's actual hook, tree and fruit listed as shape-concepts read off the arrangement of the elements (C084-M:L13), and 'heaps' becomes 'halves' in beats 5 and 8, the human question and two_layers; beat 6's 'a whole put together out of parts' becomes 'a name laid over body and mind taken together'. (6) The railed slab, the stupa and the rock are each named as the meeting spot by different accounts, and the figures at the terrace edge are described differently; both conflicts are now in what_is_disputed. (7) The Brahmi inscription, the view of the old capital's domes and the 300 m height are hedged and listed as could-not-confirm in the research note. (8) The connection notes to IDEA-0007 (which wrongly said same district and a working tank cascade) and IDEA-0002 (which described a coir film that no longer exists) now match those records. (9) The research note states that Anuradhapura District is at nine films, over the closed line of seven, with three from GRP-01, and why this film holds. selection.recommendation stays 'keep'. Still unverified: which feature marks the meeting, whether a mango tree fruits on the terrace in the filming window, the view from the rock, the inscription, verse numbers, and every permission and drone question.

suggested_location.region: Anuradhapura District, North Central Province: an isolated granite hill in the dry zone about 12.5 km east of the old capital, on the road toward Trincomalee.
suggested_location.why_here: Because the story here is not a resemblance, it is the concept being administered as an examination, and the site carries a name meaning the object in the question. C084 turns on holding apart a name, the class a name creates, and the particular thing in front of you; the chronicle records a king being tested on precisely that, with a tree, before he was allowed to be taught, and the terrace is called the mango place, a name the chronicle already uses a chapter before the question. The spot is marked, in one account, by a slab of bare rock inside a low railing, with mango trees planted around it, which gives the film a physical object at the exact centre of the argument without anything having to be staged. And the place carries the frame. The stairway is a long series of broad granite flights under frangipani; the terrace is an open sand floor with a double ring of tall octagonal pillars standing roofless around a small white dome; and the invitation rock is a single unbroken granite dome that hands the film its wide shot from the ground, which matters because the whole plain, with the distant stupas of the old capital on the skyline, is what beats three and four are pointing at. Nowhere else in the group gives the concept's own question as recorded history and a frame worth the trip in one place.

historical_thread.story: The Mahavamsa, in the chapter on the entry into the capital (chapter XIV), records the meeting on which the arrival of Buddhism on the island is dated. King Devanampiya Tissa, out hunting, came up Missaka-pabbata attended by forty thousand men, pursuing what the chronicle calls 'the deva of the mountain … in the form of an elk-stag', and found the thera Mahinda, who had come from the mainland — through the air, the chronicle says. In the chapter before (XIII), the chronicle has already set Mahinda down 'on the pleasant Missaka-mountain, on the Sila-peak on the open and fair Ambatthala', so the name exists in its narrative before the riddle is asked. Mahinda showed himself alone first, so as not to frighten the king, called him by name, and told him they were samanas, disciples of the King of Truth. Then, before teaching him anything, he tested him. 'To test him that most wise thera now asked a subtle question, and even as he was questioned the monarch answered the questions severally.' Pointing at a tree close at hand: 'What name does this tree bear, O king?' 'This tree is called a mango.' 'Is there yet another mango beside this?' 'There are many mango-trees.' 'And are there yet other trees besides this mango and the other mangoes?' 'There are many trees, sir; but those are trees that are not mangoes.' 'And are there, beside the other mangoes and those trees which are not mangoes, yet other trees?' 'There is this mango-tree, sir.' 'Thou hast a shrewd wit, O ruler of men!' He then ran the same ladder again with people: 'Hast thou kinsfolk, O king?' 'They are many, sir.' 'And are there also some, O king, who are not kinsfolk of thine?' 'There are yet more of those than of my kin.' 'Is there yet any one besides the kinsfolk and the others?' 'There is yet myself, sir.' 'Good! thou hast a shrewd wit, O ruler of men!' Only then, 'when he had known that he was a keen-witted man, the wise thera preached to the monarch the Culahatthipadupamasuttanta' — the lesser discourse on the simile of the elephant's footprint — and at the end of it the king and the forty thousand took the three refuges. The upper terrace of the hill is called Ambasthala, the mango place, a name usually explained by that tree; one account marks the spot of the dialogue by a slab of rock enclosed by a railing, with mango trees planted in the vicinity to commemorate it, while another says the stupa itself stands where Mahinda stood. The small dagoba on the terrace, the Ambasthala dagoba or Sela Cetiya, is attributed to King Mahadatika Mahanaga (9–21 CE) and was later enclosed in a vatadage, a circular stupa-house, whose two rows of slender octagonal stone pillars, about twelve feet high with carved capitals, still stand roofless around it. A headless standing Buddha and a much-worn figure identified as the king are described at the edges of the terrace, though one site description has both figures headless. Beside the terrace is the Aradhana Gala, the rock of invitation, a bare granite dome now climbed by an iron handrail, traditionally the place where Mahinda came down. The hill, which the chronicle calls Missaka-pabbata and later sources Cetiyapabbata, was given to the order; the king is said to have prepared sixty-eight cave dwellings on it, and an early Brahmi inscription on one cave near the Kantaka Cetiya is reported to record its preparation by one of the king's brothers. The way up is a ceremonial stairway of broad granite steps, commonly given as about 1,840 in all, in flights separated by terraces and lined with frangipani.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: The examination is C084's distinction, put as four questions. The first question separates the two things the Pradeepika says paññatti covers at once: a tree, which is what gets made known, and 'mango', which is what does the making known. The second turns the word into a class, so that it stops belonging to the tree it was just used on. The third builds the complementary class, defined by the name it fails, which between them exhaust every tree in sight. The fourth asks whether anything survives that, and its whole force is that the logically tidy answer is no: the categories look as if they have used up the world. The king's answer refuses to let them. 'There is this mango tree, sir' puts the particular back after the general has apparently accounted for it, which is the one move the taxonomy cannot make for itself. Then the second round applies the identical ladder to a person and ends on 'there is yet myself' — and the concept of a being is an item on the sources' own list of meaning-concepts, alongside the collective whole. That is why this hill rather than any tree: a man was tested on whether he could hold a name, a class and a particular apart, and he was tested before he was allowed to be taught, which makes the distinction a precondition of the teaching rather than a curiosity inside it. The frame closes with what followed. The discourse Mahinda chose once the king had passed was a simile about an elephant's footprint — conventional teaching in everyday images, which the Pradeepika says was used on purpose so that listeners could understand easily. The first lesson this chronicle gives on this hill was given with a tree and a footprint, in ordinary words, by a teacher who had just satisfied himself that his pupil knew the difference between a word and a thing.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: That the Mahavamsa contains this exchange, in the chapter on the entry into the capital (XIV), and that the wording quoted above is Geiger's standard English translation of it, including 'There is this mango-tree, sir' and 'Thou hast a shrewd wit, O ruler of men!', the kinsfolk sequence ending 'There is yet myself, sir', and the naming of the Culahatthipadupama Sutta as the discourse that followed. That the same chapter frames the meeting with the mountain's deva in the form of an elk-stag and has the monks arrive through the air, and that the preceding chapter (XIII) already names the landing place 'the open and fair Ambatthala'. That the chronicle names the hill Missaka-pabbata and gives the king's escort as forty thousand men. That the upper terrace and its stupa are called Ambasthala, the mango place. That the stupa on the terrace stands inside a double ring of surviving octagonal stone pillars from a vatadage. That the Aradhana Gala is a bare granite dome beside the terrace with an iron handrail up it. That the hill is a living pilgrimage site with a granite stairway up it, commonly given as about 1,840 steps.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed: Above all: this is chronicle, not documented event. The Mahavamsa was compiled in the fifth or sixth century CE, from the Dipavamsa and monastic tradition, about a meeting placed in the third century BC, and its own account of that meeting includes a mountain deity in the form of a stag, arrival through the air, and a novice whose proclamation was heard over the whole island and as far as the brahma world. The film treats the exchange as what the chronicle records and never as reportage. The date of the meeting is given variously in secondary accounts, commonly around 247 or 246 BC. Whether the railed slab marks the actual spot is tradition and not an archaeological finding; the terrace's identification with the meeting rests on the chronicle and on the name. Accounts differ on the Ambasthala dagoba: it is attributed to Mahadatika Mahanaga (9–21 CE), with the vatadage put in the second or third century CE and sometimes credited to Kanittha Tissa (164–192 CE), and it is said both to enshrine relics of Mahinda and to enshrine the Buddha's urna roma, the hair between the eyebrows — a large stupa elsewhere on the hill is also given the hair relic. The step count of about 1,840 is the figure in common circulation and varies with which flights are counted, some accounts splitting it into roughly a thousand steps to the middle terrace and the rest above. Verse numbering for the passage was not confirmed: the standard English translation available online prints the exchange as unnumbered prose, and the chapter number XIV is certain while the verse numbers are not. Whether the mango trees now on the terrace are a continuous planting or a modern commemorative one is not established in the sources consulted. Where the name comes from: the standard site accounts explain Ambasthala, the mango place, by the tree in the riddle, but the chronicle's own narrative already uses the name in chapter XIII, when Mahinda alights 'on the Sila-peak on the open and fair Ambatthala', before the king has arrived or any question has been asked; so the name is older than the riddle in the chronicle's own telling, and the film may say exactly that and no more. Which feature marks the meeting: one account has the railed slab of rock, another (amazinglanka) says the Ambasthala stupa itself was built 'on the very spot where Mahinda Thero … stood', and the same site's page on the hill puts the encounter at the Aradhana Gala; the record does not choose. The figures at the terrace's edge: this record describes a headless standing Buddha and a much-worn figure of the king, while amazinglanka describes a Buddha 'missing its head and arms' and a figure believed to represent the king also 'missing arms and head'; neither identification has been checked against an archaeological report. Whether the chronicle's lesson here was the first on the island is the chronicle's framing only: its own first chapter has the Buddha visit the island and preach before this, so the film says 'the first lesson this chronicle gives here' and never 'the first lesson on this island'.

what_to_film: The mango tree with real fruit on it, at three distances: one fruit hanging, filling the frame, with the pillars soft behind it; the whole tree on the terrace edge, ordinary and in full sun; and the fruit against the sky. This is the spine of the film and the schedule is built around the fruiting weeks, not the other way round.
The slab of bare rock inside its railing, low and close, with a pillar shadow crossing it, filmed barefoot and without moving anything on or around it.

The terrace whole: the small dome, the double ring of roofless octagonal pillars, the open sand, the long shadows at either end of the day, and the worn figures at the edges, framed without adjudicating who they are.

The plain from the top of the granite rock, in two versions: wide enough that the forest reads as an uncountable number of trees, and long enough to pick individual crowns out of it one at a time. These shots carry beats three and four and must work without any aerial footage.
The far skyline with the white domes of the old capital standing out of the forest, at the hour they separate from the haze.
The bare granite dome itself, from the terrace, in low light, with its handrail and nothing else on it; and a static wide of it empty, which is beat six's picture.
The stairway from the bottom, looking straight up the line of a flight, with frangipani either side and flowers on the stone, at first light when it is misted and nearly empty.

The reverse move for the last beat: plain to forest to terrace to slab to tree to one fruit, in one continuous descent, at last light. If it cannot be done as a single move it is cut to look continuous and never composited.
Heat: the shake coming off the granite at midday, and bare feet on hot stone, filmed without making anybody's discomfort a subject.
suggested_location.access: A public archaeological and religious site with a ticket office at the foot; the upper terrace is a place of worship, reached on foot only, up the stone stairway in flights with terraces between them. Shoes and hats come off before the upper terrace and there is a dress expectation. The Aradhana Gala is climbed by an iron handrail up bare rock and is exposed, hot and slippery in rain. The Department of Archaeology is the site authority and filming beyond ordinary visitor photography needs its permission; the resident monastic custodians govern the terrace itself. Drone flight would additionally need Civil Aviation Authority approval and Ministry of Defence security clearance with a site no-objection letter, and over a sacred site that letter is the part most likely to be refused.
suggested_location.best_time: The mango fruiting weeks, roughly March to June in this part of the dry zone, since the close-ups need fruit on the tree. Within the day, the first and last hour of light for the stairway, the rock, the plain and the pillar shadows, and the middle of the day only for the heat. Deliberately outside the Poson full-moon period, when the hill takes very large crowds overnight and the terrace cannot be filmed quietly; that period belongs to a different idea on the slate and this film keeps clear of it entirely.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only. The chronicle passage is quoted from the Geiger translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk and cross-read against mahavamsa.org; chapter XIV is certain, verse numbers were not confirmed because the online text prints the exchange as unnumbered prose. The coordinates given are the site coordinate on the Mihintale Wikipedia article (8 deg 21 min 02.14 sec N, 80 deg 31 min 01.00 sec E), independently corroborated by the GPS tag on the Commons photograph of the Aradhana Gala listed above (8.350594, 80.516944); they locate the upper terrace and the rock beside it, and no surveyed point for the railed slab itself was found. The elevation of 300 m is the hill's commonly given height (1,000 ft) and not a measurement of the terrace. The railed rock slab, the commemorative mango trees, the terrace name, the pillar count and heights, the attributions of the stupa and the vatadage, the sixty-eight caves and the step count are all from the site descriptions listed above and are secondary sources, not the archaeological reports; where they disagree that is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than resolved. Whether a mango tree with fruit on it currently stands on or immediately beside the terrace has not been verified, and beats two, seven and eight depend on it. Commons yielded nothing that shows the railed slab or a mango tree on the terrace, so no image here claims to; the five images verified are the terrace and stupa, the granite rock, and one flight of the stairway, each confirmed to exist through the Commons query API before its URL was written. Permission routes for filming and for drone flight are from the general guidance cited and have not been tested for this site; the fruiting window, current crowd levels and custodial conditions are unverified. Corrected on 26 September 2026 after a GRP-01 audit, with the Geiger text of chapters XIII and XIV re-read at lakdiva.org.lk and the amazinglanka site pages re-read. Could not confirm, and so kept out of the voice or hedged: the early Brahmi inscription near the Kantaka Cetiya and its attribution to one of the king's brothers; whether the white domes of the old capital are actually visible from the Aradhana Gala, and on which days of haze (the on-screen note for beat four is now conditional on it); the 300 m elevation, which is the hill's commonly given 1,000 ft and not a measurement; the 'first lesson on the island' framing, which the chronicle's own first chapter contradicts; and which feature on the terrace marks the meeting. The line about everyday words chosen so listeners could follow comes from the Abhidhammartha Pradipika of Amaradasa Ratnapala, a modern Sinhala commentary, so the voice now says 'one of these books' and not 'one of the old commentaries'. District budget: Anuradhapura District stands at nine films on the slate, above the closed line of seven, and GRP-01 alone puts three there (IDEA-0002, IDEA-0008, IDEA-0012). This film holds anyway because its location is not interchangeable: the story is a chronicled examination on exactly C084's distinction, at the named spot where the chronicle sets it, and no other district carries that story. The cost is stated rather than hidden, and if the district has to lose a film, this should not be the one chosen by default.

unknowns: No custodian, official or permission has been approached. Everything here is a research direction.
Whether there is a mango tree in fruit on or immediately beside the terrace, and in which weeks, has not been checked on the ground. Three beats depend on it and there is no honest substitute.

Drone permission over a sacred site is genuinely uncertain and may well be refused: it requires a Civil Aviation Authority approval, a Ministry of Defence security clearance and a no-objection letter from the site authority, and the last of those is the likely refusal. The film is therefore designed so that the bare granite rock supplies the high ground and every wide shot can be made from it on a tripod; no beat is written that only a drone can deliver.
Whether filming on the upper terrace can be permitted at all, and on what conditions about footwear, positions, times of day and proximity to worship, is unknown.
The current condition of the railed enclosure and whether the slab can be filmed close and low without entering the railing has not been established.
How busy the terrace is on an ordinary morning in the fruiting months, as against the festival period the film is avoiding, is unverified.

The verse numbers of the passage in the chronicle, and whether the Pali wording of the four questions differs in force from the English translation used here, need a reader of the edition. The chapter numbers are certain: XIII for Mahinda alighting on Ambatthala, XIV for the hunt, the stag and the questions.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Chathura's chosen replacement; its supporting detail, the site descriptions and the reading of the chronicle are desk research and unverified, and the chronicle itself is a chronicle rather than documentary evidence of the meeting it reports. No scene or shot is decided here.
